items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And Kenny Dorham got up from his chair next to Bird and he was starting to play his solo, and I started to leave the bandstand.

ctx.x: But I couldn’t believe that and so I says whoa, man. So when I landed in Baltimore I immediately went to the nearest record shop and the guy told me where I could find Bird and Diz’s records. Because they weren’t sold in the respectable music shops. You had to go to the little dedicated jazz people to buy these records. So I bought as many of them as I could get my hands on and I bought anything that had to do with bebop, and bought Dave Lambert and Buddy Stewart. Because at that time in the store you could go in…
Kenny Dorham had just replaced Miles. So Bird had finished playing and he told me, so that I scatted. I scatted about ten choruses. I didn’t know when to stop. I was looking for a place to stop.

items.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: and he motioned me to Kenny Dorham’s chair, who had started his solo, which was going to be about 10 choruses.

ctx.x: Did he ask you what you wanted to sing?

No. They played The Song is You, and he just – he motioned to me like that. So after Kenny Dorham got through – no, after he got through, he was motioning to me. So I walked up on the stage, and I scatted on The Song is You. He heard me make those Art Tatum changes, because that’s where he was from. After I was through, my knees were knocking. I was so nervous, I thought I was going to faint. All I wanted to do was get off that stage. Let me out of here. Because these cats, man – Tommy Potter, Max Roach, Al Haig…
Was that a milestone for you? How did that affect you?
